title: Scattering and Schmid-Bulgadaev Transition in Qubits Based on Josephson Junction Chains
authors: Sviatoslav D. Krasin, Alexey Radkevich, Emil Rizvanov, Andrew G. Semenov
abstract: A Josephson junction subject to an ohmic dissipative environment undergoes a zero-temperature quantum phase transition called Schmid-Bulgadaev transition form an insulating state to a superconducting state upon increasing the impedance of the environment above the resistance quantum. Superconducting qubits based on Josephson junction chains represent a system where it is possible to dynamically explore both sides of this transition by probing the scattering of individual plasma modes of the junction chain on a SQUID at the boundary which was achieved in recent experiments. Here, we provide a theoretical analysis of the scattering in the system paying special attention to the non-perturbative superconducting regime. We find that in this regime, a specific diagrammatic resummation must be performed in order to correctly account for fluctuation renormalization of the SQUID's potential. We find analytic expressions for the modes' frequency shifts and quality factors which together provide a full description of scattering. We argue that the non-perturbative nature of the superconducting phase manifests itself through a power-law dependence of the frequency shifts on the SQUID flux and through non-monotonous dependence of the quality factors on the mode frequency. Our predictions may be readily verified in modern low-temperature experiments.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the Schmid-Bulgadaev quantum phase transition in superconducting qubits coupled to an environment. By using advanced field-theoretic methods, the authors predict unique, non-perturbative signatures—such as power-law flux dependence in frequency shifts—that characterize the superconducting phase. These predictions offer a concrete theoretical roadmap for interpreting modern low-temperature quantum experiments.
main_problem: The paper investigates the zero-temperature quantum phase transition known as the Schmid-Bulgadaev transition in superconducting qubits built from Josephson junction chains.
main_result: The authors derive analytic expressions showing that in the non-perturbative superconducting regime, frequency shifts exhibit a power-law dependence on the SQUID flux, and quality factors show non-monotonous dependence on mode frequency.
method: The analysis employs the Keldysh formalism and advanced diagrammatic resummation techniques to handle non-perturbative effects across the quantum phase transition.
model_or_system: The system consists of a Josephson junction chain terminated by a SQUID (qubit) and coupled to an external environment modeled as a transmission line. The dynamics are analyzed using an effective action derived from the circuit Lagrangian.
key_observables: Frequency-dependent reflection coefficient $S_{11}(\omega)$, mode frequency shifts ($\delta\omega_n$), and internal quality factors ($Q_{int}(\omega)$).
important_parameters: The critical environmental impedance crossing the resistance quantum ($R_Q$), the SQUID flux, and the coupling strength parameter $g$ relative to the critical value of 4.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system is electrically insulated from its surroundings and neglects phase slips occurring within the bulk of the junction chain.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the electrical circuit setup: a JJ chain connected to a SQUID qubit and an antenna. Figure 2 depicts the equivalent setup for plasma-wave scattering, defining the reflection coefficient $r(\omega)$.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the circuit model and Lagrangian formulation, moves through deriving the effective action using the Keldysh technique, and culminates in the non-perturbative analysis of scattering observables like frequency shifts and quality factors.
why_interesting: The study provides deep theoretical insight into how quantum dissipation drives a phase transition in superconducting circuits, offering measurable predictions for low-temperature experiments relevant to quantum measurement and coherence.
